## The question

Duty is not spread evenly across an import book. A small number of tariff lines
usually carry most of the cost, and those lines are where reclassification
review, first sale valuation, or a sourcing change pays for itself.

The question is where to look first, and how much a plausible change is worth
before anyone spends time on it.

## The data

  <dd>
    Aggregate national data, not any one importer's entries. Section 301 and
    IEEPA rates change; this reflects the schedule as of [date]. Rates of duty

    aggregate data flattens.
  </dd>
</dl>
:::

## Approach

[Sketch, to replace with what you actually did:]

- Load HTS-level import value and duty into SQLite, keyed on the 10-digit code.
- Join the applicable general rate, plus any Section 301 or IEEPA additional
  rate, on the chapter or subheading.
- Compute effective duty rate per line, and rank by absolute duty paid rather
  than by rate — a 2% rate on a large line beats a 25% rate on a small one.
- Model one or two concrete scenarios: shifting origin for the top lines, or
  reclassifying where the code looks contestable.

```{sql}
#| eval: false
select substr(hts_code, 1, 4)          as heading,
       sum(customs_value)              as value,
       sum(calculated_duty)            as duty,
       sum(calculated_duty) * 1.0
         / nullif(sum(customs_value), 0) as effective_rate
from imports
where year = 2025
group by heading
order by duty desc
limit 20;
```

## What I found

[Result and one chart. Rank chapters by duty, and show effective rate against
value so the outliers are visible.]

## What I would do differently

[Name the weakness. Likely candidates: aggregate data hides origin mix, the
scenarios assume a sourcing change is feasible when qualification and lead time
often make it not, and duty is only part of landed cost.]
